lead.headline: Archon II: Adept brings a new war of magic to home computers
lead.dek: Electronic Arts’ strategy-and-action sequel earns an enthusiastic August review.
body: The battlefield is magical, but the accounting is exacting. Archon II: Adept, developed by Free Fall Associates and published by Electronic Arts, earns an enthusiastic review from Arthur Leyenberger in August’s COMPUTE! The sequel keeps the mixture of strategic planning and real-time fighting while changing the armies and the decisions that sustain them.

Pieces and spells draw on magical energy. Occupying power points replenishes that resource; holding every power point wins the contest. Four elemental piece types can be summoned by each side, and the element in which a fight takes place changes a unit’s effectiveness. Choosing a battle therefore begins before either player moves the joystick.

Even the spells demand restraint. Imprison requires continuing energy expenditure, making indiscriminate use costly. Apocalypse is an expensive last-resort gamble. Difficulty settings alter starting energy and combat speed, so the same board can test both deliberate planning and quick hands.

Leyenberger’s verdict is that “Archon II: Adept is even better than Archon.” The reviewed versions cost $33 for Commodore and Atari, and $40 for Apple. Requirements listed are a Commodore 64 or 128, an Atari 400/800 or XL with at least 48K, or an Apple II-series machine with at least 48K; all require a disk drive and joystick. This is August review coverage, not a newly established release date for this week.

stories.headline: Epyx lines up winter sports, Lucasfilm adventures and a dungeon trilogy
body: Epyx has a crowded program for the home-computer shelf. Tom R. Halfhill’s Summer CES report in August’s COMPUTE! lists Winter Games, a sequel to Summer Games, for Commodore 64, Apple and Macintosh. The report is a look at the company’s announced pipeline, not confirmation that every version is now in shops.

The Atari line includes the Lucasfilm games The Eidolon and Koronis Rift. The World’s Greatest Football Game is listed for Commodore 64, Apple and Atari, while Temple of Apshai Trilogy spans those machines as well as Macintosh and IBM in the announcement.

The roundup quotes a collective $19–$35 range without assigning an individual price to each title. Sports, exploration and dungeon adventuring give Epyx several different bids for the family software budget; the platform lists remain announcements rather than a shipping calendar.

stories.headline: Atari demonstrates an encyclopedia on one optical disc
body: A shelf of reference books has become a disc in Atari’s demonstration with Activenture. August’s COMPUTE! reports a working CD-ROM prototype connected to a 520ST at June’s Chicago Summer CES. The demonstration holds a 23-volume, nine-million-word encyclopedia and its index on one disc.

Even after that load, the account says three quarters of the disc remains empty. Activenture engineering vice president Tom Rolander emphasizes indexing: retrieving a passage may matter as much as storing it. This is read-only storage, not a new way for home users to record their own files.

Atari hopes for a product late in 1985 or early 1986 at about $500. That is a forecast, not a current retail offer. The encyclopedia publisher remains unnamed because the final contract has not been signed; the demonstration shows technical promise while publishing and pricing remain unfinished business.

stories.headline: Commodore fills out the 128’s peripheral shelf
body: The Commodore 128’s future extends beyond the keyboard in August’s CES reporting. COMPUTE! describes the 1572 as two 1571 drives in a slim case intended to sit atop the 128, supporting Commodore 64, 128 and CP/M formats. Summer availability is promised, but a price is not supplied.

The MPS 1000 printer is rated at 100 characters per second in draft and 16 in near-letter-quality mode. The report lists 50–240 dots per inch graphics and widths of 80–160 columns, giving home-office buyers several specifications to weigh alongside software compatibility.

Communications gets the 1670 direct-connect modem, quoted around $200 with 1200-bps transfer, autodial, autoanswer and automatic 300/1200 switching. A two-button mouse is announced at $49.95. These are June show promises carried in August’s magazine, not independently confirmed deliveries during this week.

computerItems.title: Amstrad CPC6128 planned for US
computerItems.summary: August CES report p.18: Z80A, 128K, built-in 3-inch drive, CP/M compatibility, BASIC and Logo, joystick and stereo output. US configurations announced at $699 with green monitor and WordStar, or $799 with RGB monitor, Amstrad word processor and entertainment software; scheduled later in year, not a confirmed target-week shipment.

computerItems.summary: August pp.20–22 preview, written early June: Motorola 68000, 256K RAM, multitasking, custom graphics, 4096-color palette and four-voice stereo. Useful background only; do not repeat provisional 192K ROM/Intuition packaging or price rumors as final specifications.

market.headline: A large installed base meets a busy new-machine season
market.summary: Publishers and peripheral makers are announcing versions across established 8-bit computers and newer machines. Epyx’s platform lists, Commodore’s accessories and Atari’s optical-disc forecast show competing bids for household spending; announcements are not proof of stock or sales.

worldAnchor.headline: Hiroshima anniversary renews nuclear debate
worldAnchor.summary: On August 6, Ronald Reagan marked forty years since the atomic bombings, urged arms reductions and reiterated his invitation for Soviet experts to observe and measure a US nuclear test. His statement presented deterrence as part of the administration’s argument, not a settled answer to the nuclear debate.

bbsNote.headline: The online clubs are becoming a business
bbsNote.summary: Arlan R. Levitan’s Telecomputing Today: SIGs: Behind the Scenes (COMPUTE!, August 1985, p.33) describes commercial discussion communities, sysop compensation and competition among services. These are reported contemporary estimates, not audited accounts. These posts summarize printed reporting, not fabricated historical board messages.

posts.platform: CompuServe and other commercial information services
posts.text: Levitan divides SIGs into topic message areas, file databases for software and saved messages, and real-time conferences. His column says older messages can disappear within a week as new ones overwrite them.

The column says leading SIGs gross more than $1 million annually and a head sysop or sponsor may receive at least 5 percent, while assistants often receive free SIG time. These are the columnist’s claims; no specific operator is identified.

Levitan says Delphi and The Source are entering the SIG business. He recounts an unnamed Commodore SIG staff moving to a competitor and another unnamed community splitting after a sysop dispute; do not invent service identities or board names.
The CES roundup p.15 quotes Commodore’s 1670 direct-connect 1200-bps modem at around $200, with autoanswer and automatic 300/1200 switching.

curiosity.headline: An encyclopedia disc with room to spare
curiosity.summary: The optical-disc demonstration in August’s COMPUTE! packs a 23-volume encyclopedia onto a disc that is still three quarters empty.
curiosity.detail: The delightful detail is accompanied by a real business problem: publishers worried consumers would value a small disc less than a shelf of books. Tom Rolander asks whether buyers would pay $500, $150 or $50 for the information. Those are rhetorical pricing questions, not an advertised encyclopedia price. Source: Halfhill, pp.14–15; demonstration took place at June CES.
